questions.explanation: The worth of a permission is what it would let an attacker do with a stolen key, and a grant that a job never uses is pure risk: the report job holding the ability to issue refunds means one leaked nightly credential can move money rather than only read totals. One tidy service does not offset that, because the excess belongs to a different key with a different owner. Nothing here is malfunctioning either: the grants work exactly as written, which is precisely why no alert fires and no test fails, and a permission that is never exercised cannot announce its own danger.

questions.explanation: The sequence also works as an inventory of what the attacker held at each step: after the first, unauthenticated reach on the service; after the second, the ability to steer a query rather than merely send text; after the third, a copy of a record they were never meant to see; after the fourth, a way to have their own code run in every later reader's browser. Each step is also a place where one control would have broken the chain, which is what makes the timeline useful rather than merely narrative: validating shape, binding values, checking authorisation, and escaping on output are four separate chances. Ordering them this way shows which chance came first and which were never taken.

questions.topic: What an incident timeline says the attacker already had

answer.exemplar: Every internal service trusting the network makes the firewall the only thing distinguishing an attacker from a colleague, so the moment one machine on that network is compromised, everything the firewall was protecting is reachable through that single path. The design has no depth because its layers are not independent: they all inherit the same assumption, which is why adding a second tool that also trusts the network changes nothing. A real second layer changes the arithmetic rather than the paperwork, so a service that authenticates its own callers and grants only what each one needs means a foothold on one host buys a foothold on one host, and a stolen credential for a nightly report cannot reach card numbers. Depth also means the layers fail differently, which is why encryption at rest, a separate administration path, per-service credentials and a log the user cannot quietly edit belong together. None of it makes a breach impossible; it bounds how far one mistake travels, and that bound is the difference between an incident and a catastrophe.

questions.explanation: Depth only counts when the layers fail independently, and layers that share an assumption are one control wearing several hats: a firewall plus services that trust the network plus a log the network can edit is still a single decision, and it fails as one. The value of a second layer is that it changes the arithmetic of a compromise, bounding how far one foothold travels rather than adding another object to a checklist. That is why per-service credentials, encryption at rest, a separate administration path and logs a user cannot quietly alter belong together, since each fails for a different reason.
questions.hint: Ask what the second layer does to the blast radius rather than to the list of controls.
